title: Samsung Texas Plant to Make HBM Parts for AMD, Nvidia: Report
excerpt: Samsung's second Taylor plant will reportedly produce HBM base dies for AMD and Nvidia using 2-nanometre technology, with mass production expected in 2030, Maeil reported — Samsung declined to comment.
body:
• Samsung's second Taylor, Texas plant will produce base dies for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips for AMD and Nvidia, South Korea's Maeil Business Newspaper reported, citing industry sources — Samsung declined to comment.
  • Construction is due to start formally this month, equipment installation is expected from February 2029, and mass production is expected in 2030, Maeil said.
  • The plant will use 2-nanometre technology, cover about 2.7 million square feet — roughly 1.5 times the first facility — and has secured orders for its entire output, most of it for AMD, according to the report.
  • Samsung's first Taylor facility has a contract with Tesla; Stocktwits put that agreement at $16.5 billion, signed in July 2025.

SEOUL — Samsung Electronics will use its second foundry plant in Taylor, Texas, to produce base dies for high-bandwidth memory chips for AMD and Nvidia, South Korea's Maeil Business Newspaper reported on Tuesday, citing industry sources, Reuters reported.

This is a reported plan, not a confirmed Samsung announcement. Samsung Electronics declined to comment on the matter, Reuters said. Readers should treat the customer, timing and output details below as Maeil's reporting, attributed to industry sources, until Samsung or the customers confirm them.

What the second plant would make

The facility would produce base dies for HBM chips. HBM is a type of memory used alongside processors in AI chips, and its high bandwidth lets large amounts of data move quickly between memory and processors, Stocktwits explained in its coverage of the report. An HBM package consists of multiple stacked memory layers, and the base die sits at the bottom of the stack and helps manage how data moves through the memory.

https://x.com/BetTheDecade/status/2117603576931328392

Samsung would manufacture those components, rather than the main processors designed by AMD and Nvidia, Stocktwits said.

Timeline, size and technology

Construction is due to start formally this month, Maeil said. Equipment is expected to be installed from February 2029, with mass production in 2030.

The plant will use advanced 2-nanometre technology and cover about 2.7 million square feet, roughly 1.5 times the size of the first facility, Maeil said. It has secured orders for its entire output, and most of the secured volume is for AMD, according to Maeil.

That long timeline is the practical takeaway for investors and workers: even on the reported schedule, this is a 2030 production story, not a near-term source of HBM supply.

Tesla anchors the first plant

Samsung's first Taylor facility has a contract with Tesla, Maeil said. Stocktwits put the figure on that deal at $16.5 billion, saying Tesla signed the agreement in July 2025 to manufacture its next-generation AI chips at the facility. If the reported AMD and Nvidia orders proceed, Stocktwits said, the second plant would give Samsung's contract manufacturing business three major U.S. customers tied to AI computing.

Stocktwits also reported market moves on Tuesday morning: AMD stock was up about 2.3 per cent in pre-market trading, while Nvidia gained around 1.4 per cent. Those were Stocktwits' figures at the time of its report, not a guarantee of how the shares closed.

Samsung's Taylor footprint

Samsung's own site describes Taylor as its largest-ever investment in the United States. On its official Taylor page, Samsung puts the initial minimum investment in the Taylor fab at $17 billion, including buildings, property improvements, machinery and equipment, and says the facility will boost production of semiconductor solutions for areas including 5G, artificial intelligence and high-performance computing.

The same official page says the U.S. Department of Commerce awarded Samsung up to $4.745 billion in direct funding under the CHIPS and Science Act on December 20, 2024, and that Samsung is expected to invest more than $37 billion in the region in the coming years. That official context covers Samsung's Taylor presence in general; it does not confirm the Maeil report about AMD and Nvidia base dies at a second plant.

Why it matters

A U.S. source of HBM base dies would add a domestic link in the AI memory supply chain for two of the largest AI processor designers. For now, the claim rests on a single newspaper report citing unnamed industry sources, with no comment from Samsung and no confirmation in the Reuters report from AMD or Nvidia. Confirmation, construction milestones, and the February 2029 equipment date Maeil cited are the checkpoints to watch.
